items.stem: A dog lies down. Five seconds later, after it has already stood back up and wandered toward the door, you say "good dog" and hand over a treat. What did you most likely just reinforce?

options.text: Lying down, since that is the behavior you meant to reward
Standing up and wandering toward the door, since that is what the dog was doing
Nothing at all, since five seconds is too short a gap to matter
The word "good dog", since dogs learn words before actions

items.stem: In one sentence, what is a marker (such as a clicker or a word like "yes") actually for in dog training?

You are shaping a dog to spin in a full circle. It now reliably does a half-turn every time you ask. You are still marking and treating a half-turn, the step you started with weeks ago. What should you do next?

options.text: Keep marking the half-turn, since it is already working well
Stop marking the half-turn and only mark a bigger turn from now on
Mark both the half-turn and any bigger turn, to be generous
Switch to marking the word "spin" instead of the turn itself

items.stem: A neighbor says their dog only sits on command because it gets a treat every time, and calls this "bribery" rather than real training. What is the actual issue, in one sentence?
AVSAB's review of the research on dog training methods found that, compared with correction-based methods (leash jerks, prong collars, shock collars), reward-based methods are:

options.text: Better for easy behaviors only, with corrections needed for the hard ones
Roughly equal in welfare and effectiveness, so either is fine
Worse for welfare but faster for effectiveness, a real tradeoff
Better for welfare and effectiveness, with no exception carved out
